findings.title: Cleanup job interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute for all jobs
findings.body: The ticker in CleanUpService.Run was changed from time.Minute*10 to time.Minute*1. This is unrelated to the annotation deadlock fix described in the PR and is not mentioned in the description. It causes every cleanup job to run 10x more frequently: deleting expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, expiring user invites, deleting stale short URLs, and two rounds of query-history deletions every minute. This is a significant increase in recurring database load across the whole system, and it also changes user-visible timing semantics (e.g., temp files and expired resources are now purged within ~1 minute instead of ~10). If this change is intentional to compensate for the cleanup now potentially under-deleting, it should be called out and justified; otherwise it should be reverted or scoped to annotations only.

findings.title: Normal cleanup progress logged at Error level with full ID lists
findings.body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log each batch via r.log.Error (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579), e.g. r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err). These are informational progress messages, not errors (err is nil at the points where it is logged), so every cleanup cycle now emits error-severity log lines, which will trip log-based alerting on errors. Worse, each line includes the complete ID slice, which is up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries — a batch size of 32767 produces ~200KB log lines, twice per batch, and with the cleanup interval now at 1 minute this happens every minute. These look like leftover debug statements and should be demoted to Debug and/or have the raw ID list removed.

findings.title: O(n^2) string building when inlining IDs for SQLite
findings.body: In deleteByIDs, the SQLite branch builds the IN list with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside a loop over ids. Each iteration copies the entire accumulated string, so for a batch of N ids the total copied bytes grow quadratically — with the tested batch size of 32767 this is on the order of gigabytes of allocation/copying for a single DELETE. Use a strings.Builder (or strings.Join on a converted slice) to build the list in linear time.
